catalog_quote: Stress is contrastive in Takestani words and partly predictable from word class and shape. Stress in nouns is generally ultimate (e.g., /peˈrʌ/ ‘brother’) unless in nouns ending with the feminine suffix -ɛ (e.g., /zɛjˈni.ɛ/ ‘woman’). Most adverbs and adjectives, like nouns, are stressed on their last syllable, such as [pøland-pøˈland] ‘loud-loud (loudly)’ and [qaˈʃank] ‘beautiful.’ Adpositions are primarily mono-syllabic and are typically cliticized to a nominal complement, which is stressed. An example is the noun-postposition – [zʌˈrine rʌ] ‘child for (for the child)’ in which the nominal component [zʌˈrin] rather than the adposition rʌ is stressed. At the phrase level, nouns attract stress, so adverbs and adjectives are typically less prominent overall. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress is on the final syllable (nouns, adjectives, adverbs, present-tense verbs); the feminine suffix -ɛ is unstressed so feminine nouns are stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stress the stem; monosyllabic adpositions are clitics and unstressed. Stress is therefore morphologically conditioned and contrastive in a few morphological minimal pairs (/vɛˈjɛ/ 'wedding' vs /ˈvɛj-ɛ/ 'bride'; /uˈvaz/ 'dancer' vs /ˈuvaz/ 'dance!'), but the placement is predictable from word class and morphology. Yar-Shater 1969 (§§82-83, pp. 57-58) agrees for the whole Southern Tati group: 'All uninflected masculine nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; 'All plural oblique nouns are stressed on the final syllable'; stress 'distinctive' yet 'generally predictable', and 'weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation'.
new_statements.exceptions: Feminine nouns in -ɛ (older -a) stressed on the penult; past-tense verbs stem-stressed; adpositions cliticized and unstressed; verb stress governed by 'stress-attracting morphemes that compete for stress in a hierarchy' (details declared beyond the study's scope); Yar-Shater 1969: compounds keep only the second member's stress; imperfect stresses the last syllable of the past stem.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, with a note that at phrase level nouns attract stress and adjectives/adverbs are less prominent; Yar-Shater 1969 says word stress is weak and dominated by sentence stress and intonation. Acoustic cues (JIPA): higher f0 and intensity on stressed vowels; duration is not a cue (final lengthening instead).
new_statements.identity_note: The JIPA illustration describes the Takestani dialect of Southern Tati as spoken in the city of Takestan (Siyaden), Qazvin province — exactly Glottolog take1255 / ISO tks. Yar-Shater 1969 states its stress rules for 'Southern Tati' as a group (Chali, Takestani, Eshtehardi, Esfarvarini, Xiaraji, Xoznini, Danesfani, Ebrahimabadi, Sagzabadi) with Takestani examples; Glottolog/Ethnologue subsume this Ramand-Eshtehard group under take1255, so the two sources describe the same variety at different granularity.
